script.title: Provision vs Reserve
script.caption_hook: Provision and reserve look the same. They are not.

lines.say: Provision and reserve look so similar. What's the real difference?
Good question! Both keep money aside. But one is charged before profit, and the other comes after.
Before profit, after profit... what does that mean?
Your shop earns ₹1,00,000. You expect ₹10,000 of debts may go bad. Charging it leaves profit ₹90,000.
So the amount is deducted first, and then profit comes?
Yes! That's a provision. A charge against profit for a known liability or fall in asset value, estimated.
And a reserve? Is that also a charge?
No. From the ₹90,000 profit, you keep ₹20,000 aside as general reserve. That's an appropriation of profit.
Wait... what if the shop makes a loss?
A provision is still made, because it is a charge. A reserve needs profit.
Oh! Can we pay dividend from them?
Only free reserves, like general reserve, can be used for dividend. A provision cannot.
Got it! Provision is charged before profit!
Remember: provision cuts profit, and reserve uses profit already earned.

check_notes: Writer: Word count about 165. Reserve example uses general reserve (free reserve), consistent with note.

Checker: Line 2 (voice): 'Both keep money aside' is misleading. Neither a provision nor a reserve means cash is physically set aside. A provision is a charge against profit. A reserve is profit kept in the business, and it is invested outside only in a reserve fund. Correct version: 'Both set aside an amount out of profits on paper. But one is charged before profit is found, and the other is taken from profit after it is found.'

Checker: Line 4 (voice): 'Your shop earns ₹1,00,000' could be read as revenue or sales rather than profit. Correct version: 'Your shop's profit before provision is ₹1,00,000. You expect ₹10,000 of debtors may go bad. Charging this provision leaves a net profit of ₹90,000.' The arithmetic is right: 1,00,000 − 10,000 = 90,000.

Checker: Line 12 (voice): 'Only free reserves … can be used for dividend' could suggest dividend is paid only out of reserves. Dividend is mainly paid from current-year profits, and free reserves can also be used, subject to the rules. Correct version: 'Dividend comes from profits, and free reserves like general reserve can also be used. A provision can never be used for dividend.'
